Each iteration the candidate is trained on the replay buffer, then plays 10 games against the champion with colours alternating. If it scores ≥ 55% it is promoted and becomes the new champion. If not, the candidate is discarded as a generator and the champion keeps its job.

Colours alternate deliberately — a network that only wins as Black scores ~50% and cannot pass.
input.new_string:
Each iteration the candidate is trained on the replay buffer, then plays Gate Games against the champion with colours alternating. If it scores at least the Promotion Threshold it is promoted and becomes the new champion. If not, the candidate is discarded as a generator and the champion keeps its job.

Colours alternate deliberately — a network that only wins as Black scores ~50% and cannot pass.

Promotion Gate on / off

Recommended: On

Master switch for the whole mechanism. With the gate off, every trained candidate is copied straight into the champion slot, so a bad gradient step immediately starts generating the self-play data that all future iterations learn from — and nothing in the loop can detect or undo it.

On Strength can only ever ratchet upward. Costs one extra match per iteration.
Off Iterations run faster, but regressions are permanent and compound. Only useful for quick throwaway experiments.
Default: On  ·  Skipping the gate also blanks the Champion Progress chart.

Gate Games candidate vs champion

Recommended: 20–30

How many head-to-head games decide a promotion. This is a statistical measurement, and its reliability comes almost entirely from the number of games, not from how well each game is played. With only 10 games, a candidate that is genuinely 65% strength still fails the gate about 25% of the time — real progress gets thrown away as noise.

More (20–40) Sharper verdicts at every effect size: a truly worse candidate ($p = 0.35$) is blocked ~95% of the time instead of ~90%, and a truly better one ($p = 0.65$) is accepted ~88% instead of ~75%.
Fewer (2–10) Cheap gate, but the verdict is close to a coin flip — expect both lost progress and promoted regressions.
Range 2–60  ·  Default: 20  ·  Always even, so both colours are played equally.

Promotion Threshold win share required

Recommended: 0.55

The win rate the candidate must reach to take the champion's job. 0.50 would promote on a coin flip; the margin above 50% is what stops sampling noise from installing a network that is merely equal.

Higher (0.60–0.80) Only clearly-better networks get promoted. Late in training, when gains per iteration are small, this can stall the ladder completely.
Lower (0.50–0.53) Promotes readily and keeps the ladder moving, but lets sideways or slightly worse networks through, which drifts the self-play data quality downward.
Range 0.50–0.80  ·  Default: 0.55  ·  Shown as the dashed rule on the Champion Progress chart.

Gate Simulations per move in gate games

Recommended: 50

MCTS budget per move during the gate match, kept separate from the self-play setting because the gate has a different job: it only needs to rank two networks, not produce training targets. Cost is roughly $\text{games} \times \text{sims}$, so for a fixed budget, buying more games beats buying more sims per game.

Higher (100–400) Each game is played closer to the networks' true strength, but the gate starts dominating iteration time — and search increasingly masks the difference between the two networks you are trying to tell apart.
Lower (10–30) Very fast matches that lean more heavily on the raw policy head — noisier per game, but affordable enough to play many of them.
Range 10–400  ·  Default: 50  ·  ~35s/game at 100 sims vs ~18s at 50 (9×9, M2).

Stall Breaker rejections before reset

Recommended: 5

After this many consecutive rejections, the candidate is assumed to have drifted somewhere it cannot recover from, and its weights are reset back to the champion's so it retrains from a known-good point instead of deadlocking. Three such resets escalate to a collapse warning, because a loop that keeps needing them has a data problem the reset cannot fix.

Higher (8–20) Gives a candidate more room to work through a rough patch on its own — worth it with a low learning rate, where progress is genuinely slow.
Lower (2–3) Snaps back quickly, but a reset also discards whatever partial progress the candidate had made, so an over-eager setting can itself prevent promotions.
Range 2–20  ·  Default: 5  ·  The counter resets to 0 on any promotion.

Gate Workers parallel gate games

Recommended: 4

Gate games are independent of each other, so they are played across a pool of worker processes. This matters more here than anywhere else in the loop: a gate game runs two MCTS searches per move (one per network), making the gate the most expensive phase of an iteration.

More (4–8) Wall-clock time drops roughly with the number of performance cores — measured ~1.9× on an M2 Air at 4 workers. Beyond the core count, workers just contend.
1 (sequential) Runs the gate in-process. Slowest, but the safest fallback if process pools misbehave on your machine.
Range 1–8  ·  Default: 4  ·  Capped at the CPU count and at Gate Games. Self-play stays single-process on purpose (MPS does not share across processes); the gate runs on CPU, so it has no such constraint.

content.text:
Done. All four parts landed, tests pass (141), and I verified each change in the running app.

## 1. Slider overflow in modals — fixed

Reproduced it first: the sliders grid measured `clientWidth 402 / scrollWidth 707` inside the Create Model modal, so the right column and the max-value labels were cut off with a horizontal scrollbar.

Cause: grid items default to `min-width: auto`, so each `1fr` column's floor was set by the `white-space: nowrap` hint text in [`.param-hint`](web/static/css/style.css:386) — the ellipsis could never kick in. Fixed in [style.css:347](web/static/css/style.css:347) with `min-width: 0` on `.param-slider-group` / `.param-slider-meta`, and `flex: 0 1 auto` on the hint (min/max labels pinned with `flex: 0 0 auto`). Now `532 / 532` — no overflow.

## 2. Champion-vs-candidate variables, now configurable

The gate decides whether a freshly trained candidate replaces the champion — and the champion generates *all* self-play data, so these were the highest-leverage numbers in the loop and were hardcoded. Six new entries in a `gate` category in [param_bounds.py](param_bounds.py:94):

| Param | Range | Default | Effect on learning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `gate_enabled` | On/Off | On | Off = regressions become champion permanently |
| `gate_games` | 2–60 | 20 | Verdict reliability — this is where statistical power comes from |
| `gate_threshold` | 0.50–0.80 | 0.55 | Margin over a coin flip; too high stalls the ladder |
| `gate_simulations` | 10–400 | 50 | Cost is games×sims; games buy more accuracy than sims |
| `gate_stall_warning` | 2–20 | 5 | Rejections before the candidate resets to champion |
| `gate_workers` | 1–8 | 4 | Gate games played in parallel |

Because the UI is generated from `/models/api/param_bounds`, these appear automatically in Create, Edit, **and** Live Tune. I added `type: "bool"` support to [param_sliders.js](web/static/js/param_sliders.js) so `gate_enabled` renders as a toggle rather than a 0/1 slider. Wired through [`TrainingParams`](model_manager.py:40), [`Config.from_model`](config.py:322), the create/update routes, and `apply_params` (live-tunable — the gate re-reads them each iteration).

Two things I fixed while in there:
- `Config.from_model` carried a **second, stale copy** of the gate defaults (`gate_games=10`, `gate_simulations=100`) that silently overrode the documented `TrainingConfig` values (20/50) for every model. Defaults now derive from the dataclass itself via `_model_default`.

**8 cores total — 4 performance + 4 efficiency (Apple M2, 16 GB).** So the hard ceiling is 8 parallel workers, which is exactly where I set the `gate_workers` slider max.

But the useful number is higher than the 4 I defaulted to. Measured just now, 8 real gate games at 50 sims on 9×9:

| Workers | Time | Per game | vs sequential¹ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | ~144s | 18.0s | 1.0× |
| 4 | 126.1s | 15.8s | 1.1× |
| 6 | 82.7s | 10.3s | 1.7× |
| 8 | 77.8s | 9.7s | 1.9× |

¹ sequential extrapolated from the 18.0s/game I measured earlier.

Two things worth reading off that:

**4 workers scales badly here (1.1×).** That's worse than the 1.9× I measured earlier at 4 games — because with 8 games and 4 workers each worker runs two games back-to-back, and macOS parks some of them on efficiency cores, so the whole match waits on the slowest straggler. The gate finishes only when its *last* game finishes, so uneven core speed hurts more than raw core count.

**6–8 is the better setting on this machine**, and the gain from 6→8 is small (5s). I'd use **6**: it captures nearly all the speedup while leaving a core for the trainer's main process and the web server, which matters since the gate runs while the Flask/SocketIO server is serving your dashboard.

Caveats on pushing to 8:
- Each worker is a separate Python process holding both networks plus its own torch runtime — roughly 300–400 MB each, so ~3 GB at 8 workers. Fine on your 16 GB, but not free.
- It's capped at `min(gate_workers, gate_games, cpu_count)`, so setting 8 with `gate_games=6` just gives you 6.
- Larger networks (medium/large preset) shift the bottleneck toward memory bandwidth, where the E-cores contribute less — expect the 6→8 gain to shrink further there.

One related thing I did **not** change: `evaluate_against_random` hardcodes its pool at `min(num_games, cpu_count, 4)` in [evaluator.py:129](ai/evaluator.py:129) — a fixed 4, not configurable and not covered by the new slider. It's a much cheaper phase (one MCTS search per move, and the random bot's moves are free), so it wasn't the bottleneck you asked about, but if you want that on the same knob it's a two-line change.

    state = GameState(board_size=board_size, komi=komi)
    mcts = MCTS(
        network=network,
        num_simulations=num_simulations,
        c_puct=c_puct,
        device=device,
        fpu_reduction=fpu_reduction,
    )
    
    # Collect training data as we play
    # Each entry: (state_tensor, mcts_policy, player_color)
    history = []
    move_list = []  # For the game record (replay in UI)
    win_rates = []  # Black's win probability (%) at each move, for the eval curve
    
    # Pass is disabled in early game (opening/midgame) to prevent premature
    # double-pass terminations that distort area scoring and flood replay buffer
    # with fake komi wins for White.
    #
    # The cutoff is JITTERED per game. A fixed boundary is a hard legal/illegal
    # discontinuity at a known move number, and the policy head learns it as a
    # feature rather than as strategy: P(pass) measured 0.000 before the cutoff
    # and 0.4-0.5 immediately after it, with the median first pass landing
    # exactly on the cutoff move. Randomizing the boundary removes the signal
    # the network was latching onto.
    base_min_pass = int(board_size * 3.3)  # 29 moves on 9x9
    min_pass_move = max(1, base_min_pass + random.randint(-4, 6))
    
    for move_num in range(max_moves):
        if state.is_over:
            break
        
        # Temperature schedule: smooth decay from temperature_init to temperature_final
        if temperature_threshold > 0:
            progress = min(1.0, move_num / float(temperature_threshold))
            temp = temperature_init + progress * (temperature_final - temperature_init)
        else:
            temp = temperature_final
        
        # Disallow pass during opening to force stone development
        allow_pass = (move_num >= min_pass_move)
        
        # Run MCTS to get action and policy
        action, policy = mcts.search(
            state,
            temperature=temp,
            add_noise=True,  # Always add noise during training
            allow_pass=allow_pass,
        )
        
        # Store training data (before applying the move)
        state_tensor = state.encode_for_nn()
        # Store the MCTS root evaluation alongside the position. It is the
        # per-position component of the value target (see value_target_outcome_weight)
        # and is already from this mover's perspective.
        history.append((state_tensor, policy, state.current_player, mcts.root_value))
        
        # Record move for game replay
        move_list.append({
            'color': int(state.current_player),
            'move': list(action),
            'move_num': move_num,
        })

        # Record the MCTS root evaluation as Black's win probability (%).
        # mcts.root_value is from the current player's perspective in [-1, +1];
        # flip to Black's perspective, then map [-1, +1] -> [0%, 100%].
        value_black = mcts.root_value if state.current_player == BLACK else -mcts.root_value
        win_rates.append(round(50.0 + 50.0 * value_black, 1))
        
        # Apply the move
        if action == MOVE_PASS:
            state.play_pass()
        else:
            success = state.play_move(action[0], action[1])
            if not success:
                # This shouldn't happen — MCTS only returns legal moves.
                # But if it does, pass instead.
                state.play_pass()
    
    # If game didn't end naturally, force two passes
    if not state.is_over:
        state.play_pass()
        if not state.is_over:
            state.play_pass()
    
    # Determine winner
    scorer = get_scorer("chinese")
    winner_color, margin = scorer.determine_winner(state)
    black_score, white_score = scorer.score(state)
    
    # Convert history into training samples with outcomes
    # Outcome is +1 if the player at that position won, -1 if lost, 0 for draw
    #
    # IMPORTANT: Only include samples from opening + midgame (first board_size²
    # moves). Late-game filling moves produce near-uniform MCTS policy targets.
    max_training_moves = board_size * board_size  # 81 for 9x9
    samples = []
    
    # Discard samples from abnormally short games to avoid corrupting the
    # replay buffer with premature game noise. Uses the un-jittered base so the
    # discard threshold stays stable from game to game.
    if len(move_list) >= base_min_pass:
        w = value_target_outcome_weight
        for move_idx, (state_tensor, policy, player_color, root_q) in enumerate(history):
            if move_idx >= max_training_moves:
                break  # Skip late-game filler positions

            if winner_color is None:
                outcome = 0.0  # Draw
            elif player_color == winner_color:
                outcome = 1.0  # This player won
            else:
                outcome = -1.0  # This player lost

            # Blend the game outcome with this position's own search evaluation.
            # Outcome alone gives every position in a game the SAME label, so
            # when one colour wins nearly every game the label becomes
            # predictable from the turn-colour plane and the value head stops
            # reading the board entirely. root_q varies position-to-position,
            # which keeps the target grounded in the actual position.
            target = w * outcome + (1.0 - w) * float(root_q)
            samples.append((state_tensor, policy, max(-1.0, min(1.0, target))))
    
    # Build game record for storage/replay
    game_record = {
        'board_size': board_size,
        'komi': komi,
        'moves': move_list,
        'num_moves': len(move_list),
        'win_rates': win_rates,
        'winner': int(winner_color) if winner_color else 0,
        'black_score': black_score,
        'white_score': white_score,
        'margin': margin,
        'timestamp': datetime.now().isoformat(),
    }
    
    return samples, game_record


def _play_worker(kwargs: dict) -> Tuple[List[TrainingSample], dict]:
    """Worker function for multiprocessing."""
    import torch
    import time
    
    # Prevent PyTorch from spawning many threads per worker, which causes CPU thrashing
    torch.set_num_threads(1)
    
    start_time = time.time()
    samples, record = play_self_play_game(**kwargs)
    record['elapsed_seconds'] = round(time.time() - start_time, 2)
    return samples, record


def run_self_play_batch(
    network: GoNetwork,
    num_games: int,
    board_size: int = 9,
    komi: float = 6.5,
    num_simulations: int = 200,
    c_puct: float = 1.5,
    temperature_threshold: int = 15,
    device: str = "cpu",
    game_store_every_n: int = 5,
    games_dir: str = "data/games",
    iteration: int = 0,
    progress_callback: Optional[Callable] = None,
    fpu_reduction: float = 0.35,
    value_target_outcome_weight: float = 0.6,
    stop_checker: Optional[Callable[[], bool]] = None,
) -> List[TrainingSample]:
    """
    Run a batch of self-play games and return all training samples.
    
    Only stores 1 out of every `game_store_every_n` games to disk.
    All games contribute training data regardless.
    
    Args:
        network: Current neural network.
        num_games: Number of games to play.
        board_size: Board size.
        komi: Komi.
        num_simulations: MCTS simulations per move.
        c_puct: Exploration constant.
        temperature_threshold: Move number for temperature switch.
        device: Torch device.
        game_store_every_n: Save every Nth game for replay.
        games_dir: Directory to save game records.
        iteration: Current training iteration (for filename).
        progress_callback: Called after each game with (game_num, total, game_record).
        stop_checker: Function returning True if training loop wants immediate stop.
    
    Returns:
        List of all training samples from all games.
    """
    all_samples = []
    os.makedirs(games_dir, exist_ok=True)
    
    import concurrent.futures
    import multiprocessing as mp
    
    # Restrict to at most 4 parallel CPU workers to prevent thermal throttling on Macs
    num_workers = min(num_games, os.cpu_count() or 4, 4)
    
    tasks = []
    for _ in range(num_games):
        tasks.append({
            'network': network,
            'board_size': board_size,
            'komi': komi,
            'num_simulations': num_simulations,
            'c_puct': c_puct,
            'temperature_threshold': temperature_threshold,
            'device': device,
            'fpu_reduction': fpu_reduction,
            'value_target_outcome_weight': value_target_outcome_weight,
        })
    
    completed_games = 0
    with concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=num_workers) as executor:
        futures = {executor.submit(_play_worker, task): i for i, task in enumerate(tasks)}
        pending = set(futures.keys())
        
        while pending:
            if stop_checker and stop_checker():
                executor.shutdown(wait=False, cancel_futures=True)
                break
            
            done, pending = concurrent.futures.wait(
                pending, timeout=0.1, return_when=concurrent.futures.FIRST_COMPLETED
            )
            
            for future in done:
                game_index = futures[future]
                
                try:
                    samples, record = future.result()
                except Exception as e:
                    print(f"Worker failed: {e}")
                    continue
                
                record['iteration'] = iteration
                record['game_index'] = game_index

                all_samples.extend(samples)

                # Store every Nth game for replay in the web UI
                if completed_games % game_store_every_n == 0:
                    save_game(games_dir, iteration, PHASE_SELF_PLAY, game_index, record)
                
                completed_games += 1
                
                # Report progress
                if progress_callback:
                    progress_callback(completed_games, num_games, record)
    
    return all_samples

            sanitized[key] = int(clamped)
        else:
            sanitized[key] = round(clamped, 6)
    return sanitized

def sanitize_params(raw_params: dict) -> dict:
    """
    Sanitize and clamp input training parameters according to PARAM_BOUNDS.
    Returns a dict with clamped and typed values.
    """
    sanitized = {}
    for key, spec in PARAM_BOUNDS.items():
        if key not in raw_params or raw_params[key] is None:
            continue
        val = raw_params[key]
        if spec["type"] == "bool":
            # Accept real booleans, 0/1 from a slider, and "true"/"false" from
            # a JSON client that stringified the value.
            if isinstance(val, str):
                sanitized[key] = val.strip().lower() in ("1", "true", "yes", "on")
            else:
                sanitized[key] = bool(val)
            continue
        try:
            if spec["type"] == "int":
                num_val = int(round(float(val)))
            else:
                num_val = float(val)
        except (ValueError, TypeError):
            continue
        clamped = max(spec["min"], min(spec["max"], num_val))
        if spec["type"] == "int":
            sanitized[key] = int(clamped)
        else:
            sanitized[key] = round(clamped, 6)
    return sanitized

Parallel Workers all game-playing phases

Recommended: 4–6

Every phase that plays games plays them across a pool of worker processes, because games are independent of one another. One setting governs all three:

PhaseGamesCost per move
Self-play Self-Play Games One MCTS search — generates the training data.
Promotion gate Gate Games Two MCTS searches (one per network) — the most expensive phase.
Random eval Eval Games One MCTS search; the random bot's moves are free.

All three run on CPU, so none of them is affected by the MPS single-process constraint — the trainer hands them its CPU-resident champion, not the MPS training network. The effective count is $\min(\text{workers},\ \text{games in that phase},\ \text{CPU cores})$, so raising it past your game count does nothing.

More (6–8) A phase finishes only when its slowest game does, so leaving cores idle costs more than it looks. Measured on an 8-core M2 (4P + 4E), 8 gate games: 126s at 4 workers, 83s at 6, 78s at 8.
Fewer (1–3) Leaves headroom for the web server and anything else you are running, and runs cooler on a fanless laptop. 1 is the safe fallback if process pools misbehave.
Range 1–8  ·  Default: 4  ·  Each worker is a separate process holding its own copy of the network (~300–400 MB), so 8 workers costs a few GB of RAM.

# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## Commands

```bash
# Setup
python3 -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

# Run the web server (dashboard, play UI, training UI)
python run_server.py [--port PORT] [--debug]

# Run training headless from the CLI
python run_training.py [--iterations N] [--board-size 9] [--simulations 200]

# Tests (suite lives under tests/, 97+ tests)
python -m pytest tests/ -v
python -m pytest tests/test_rules.py -v          # single file
python -m pytest tests/test_rules.py::test_name -v  # single test
```

There is no linter/formatter configured in this repo (no flake8/black/ruff config).

Note: `test_mp.py`, `test_mp2.py`, and `test_socket.py` at the project root are ad-hoc debug scripts (multiprocessing experiments, a socket.io smoke-test client), not part of the pytest suite in `tests/`. Don't confuse them with real tests.

## Architecture

Three independent layers, each importable without the others pulling in unrelated deps:

- **`game/`** — pure Go rules engine, no ML or web dependencies. `board.py` (grid, groups, liberties, Zobrist hashing), `rules.py` (legality, captures, ko/superko), `game_state.py` (`GameState`: move history, undo, NN state encoding via `encode_for_nn()`), `scoring/` (pluggable `ScoringStrategy` via `get_scorer(method)` — chinese/japanese, plus a display-only `estimator.py` using Benson's algorithm + flood-fill that bots never see).
- **`ai/`** — AlphaZero-style pipeline built on top of `game/`. `network.py` (`GoNetwork`: small ResNet, policy + value heads), `mcts.py` (`MCTS`/`MCTSNode`, PUCT selection, Dirichlet root noise), `self_play.py` (plays games with MCTS + network, produces `TrainingSample = (state_tensor, mcts_policy, outcome)`), `trainer.py` (`Trainer`: orchestrates self-play → replay buffer → train → evaluate → checkpoint loop; runs in a background thread when driven from the web UI, emits progress via a callback), `evaluator.py` (Elo tracking, eval vs random bot / previous checkpoint), `checkpoint.py` (save/load `weights.pt`).
- **`web/`** — Flask + SocketIO app (`web/app.py` factory). REST blueprints: `game_routes.py` (`/play`, `/api/game/*` — new/move/bot_move/pass/resign/undo/suggest/estimate), `training_routes.py` (`/training/*`), `model_routes.py` (`/models/api/*`), `api.py` (`/api/health`, `/api/config`). Real-time training progress goes over SocketIO (`start_training`/`stop_training`/`request_status` events, `training_update` emissions), not REST polling.

### Config

`config.py` defines dataclasses (`BoardConfig`, `NetworkConfig`, `MCTSConfig`, `TrainingConfig`, `PathConfig`, bundled into `Config`) as the single source of truth for tunables. `_get_device()` auto-picks MPS > CUDA > CPU. `Config.from_model(model_info, model_dir)` builds a per-model config, routing all paths into that model's directory.

### Multi-model architecture

`model_manager.py`'s `ModelManager` owns everything under `models/`: each model is a directory (`models/<slug>/`) with its own `config.json` (board size/komi/ruleset/training hyperparams/live Elo & iteration state), `weights.pt`, `games/`, and `logs/`.

Recorded games live under `games/iter_<NNNNNN>/<phase>/`, where phase is `self-play`, `promotion` (candidate vs champion gate matches), or `eval` (champion vs random bot). `ai/game_store.py` owns that layout — writing (`save_game`), listing (`iter_game_files` / `load_game_files`), resolving a client-supplied id (`resolve_game_path`, which rejects paths escaping `games/`), and migrating the old flat `iter_000001_game_0000.json` naming (`migrate_legacy_layout`, run from `Trainer.__init__` and the games API). A game's id everywhere — API, review URLs — is its path relative to `games/`. The currently active model id is stored in `models/.active`. `web/app.py`'s `switch_model(model_id)` builds a `Config` from the model's `ModelInfo` and creates a new `Trainer` bound to that model's directory — so switching models swaps the entire training context (weights, replay data, hyperparameters) at once.

### Self-play concurrency

Self-play intentionally runs single-process on the target hardware (M2 MacBook Air) because MPS (Apple GPU) doesn't share well across processes and sequential MPS inference is already fast enough (~5-10 games/min on 9×9). A `ProcessPoolExecutor`-based parallel path exists in `self_play.py` but is meant for CPU-only setups — don't assume it's the active path without checking how it's invoked.

### Data flow for a training iteration

`Trainer.train()` (`ai/trainer.py`): run self-play games with the current `GoNetwork` + `MCTS` → push `TrainingSample`s into a fixed-size FIFO `ReplayBuffer` → sample mini-batches and train → evaluate new weights against the random bot / previous checkpoint to update Elo → persist `weights.pt` and update the model's `config.json` state (elo, kyu_rank, iteration, total_games) → emit progress events (used by both the CLI printer in `run_training.py` and the SocketIO relay in `web/app.py`).

content.text:
You were right on both counts, and checking turned up something bigger than a categorization issue.

## It's applicable to all three phases — and two of them were *already* parallel

I put it under Champion vs Candidate because that's the phase I'd just converted. But looking at how the other two actually run:

| Phase | Before | Worker count |
|---|---|---|
| Self-play | **already parallel** | `min(games, cpus, 4)` — hardcoded |
| Random eval | **already parallel** | `min(games, cpus, 4)` — hardcoded |
| Promotion gate | sequential (I fixed it) | now configurable |

So `gate_workers` was the odd one out for no good reason. All three are `ProcessPoolExecutor` over independent games with identical tradeoffs.

**Correcting something I told you last turn:** I said self-play "stays single-process on purpose (MPS doesn't share across processes)." That's what CLAUDE.md and the `self_play.py` docstring say, and I repeated it without checking. It's wrong — [`run_self_play_batch`](ai/self_play.py:283) has no sequential branch at all; the pool is the only path. The MPS rationale doesn't apply either, because `Trainer` passes its **CPU-resident** `eval_network` with `device="cpu"` to all three phases. Only `_train_network` touches MPS. I've corrected both the docstring and the CLAUDE.md section.

## What I changed

`gate_workers` → **`num_parallel_workers`** in a new **Compute & Parallelism** category, wired into all three phases. `config.TrainingConfig.num_parallel_workers` already existed with a comment calling itself "Parallel self-play workers" — and was never read by anything. It's now the single source of truth.

The hardcoded `4` caps in self-play and eval are gone, replaced by `min(num_workers, games, cpu_count)`. That matters given last turn's measurement: 4 was the *worst* of the settings I tested on your 8-core M2 (126s vs 83s at 6 workers), and it was silently capping self-play and eval too — so raising this one slider should speed up every phase of an iteration, not just the gate.

One migration detail: your `hero of time` model had `gate_workers` persisted from my earlier API test. `ModelInfo.from_dict` now carries a stored `gate_workers` over to `num_parallel_workers` rather than dropping it back to the default.

Verified: 141 tests pass, the tuner renders the new **Compute & Parallelism** category with no `gate_workers` left anywhere, and a live-tune of `num_parallel_workers: 6` round-trips to `config.json`. Info page has a new **Parallel Workers** section (with the per-phase table and the 126/83/78s measurements) in the main parameter guide, with the gate section now linking to it instead of documenting its own knob.

One judgment call worth your input: I left the default at **4** for portability, even though 6 measured clearly better on your machine. Your active model is set to 6 now. If you'd rather the default match your hardware, that's a one-line change in `param_bounds.py` and `config.py`.

content.text:
Both done.

## 1. Temperature order

The file already listed them sensibly — the reordering was happening at serialization. Flask has `app.json.sort_keys = True`, so `PARAM_BOUNDS` came back from `/models/api/param_bounds` alphabetized, and `temperature_final` sorts before `temperature_init`. Every category was rendering in key order by accident, not by intent.

Rather than rename keys or disable Flask's sorting globally, I added an explicit `order` field to each param and made [param_sliders.js](web/static/js/param_sliders.js:35) sort on it. Now reads left-to-right in the order the value actually moves:

**Temp Init (Early) → Temp Final (Late) → Temp Decay Moves**

It also fixed ordering elsewhere that was alphabetical-by-accident — the gate block now runs Promotion Gate → Gate Games → Promotion Threshold → Gate Simulations → Stall Breaker instead of scattering the threshold between simulations and stall breaker.

## 2. Worker-balance warning

An amber note appears under any phase whose game count isn't a multiple of the effective worker count, spelling out the wave layout. Your exact example renders as:

> ⚠ 9 games over 8 workers = 2 waves; the last runs 1 game with 7 workers idle.

Applies to all three pooled phases — self-play, gate, and eval — since they share the pool. Details worth noting:

- **Effective workers, not the slider value.** The pools cap at `min(workers, games, cpu_count)`, so the API now returns `cpu_count` (8 on your machine) and the warning uses the real number. Setting 8 workers on a 4-core machine wouldn't produce a misleading wave count.
- **Fewer games than workers is not flagged.** 3 games on 8 workers is one wave — nothing waits on anything, so there's no waste to report.
- **Gate warning goes quiet when the gate is off**, since that phase doesn't run.

Verified across cases: 9/8, 5/4, 7/4 and 20/6 warn correctly; 8/8, 3/8, 1/4 stay silent; toggling the gate off silences its warning. 144 tests pass, and the modal still measures `648/648` — no horizontal overflow reintroduced by the new element.

One thing I did **not** do: the warning is advisory only, it doesn't clamp or snap the sliders. Given `gate_games` steps by 2 and self-play by 1, auto-snapping to a multiple would fight you while dragging. Say the word if you'd rather it round to the nearest multiple on release.

content.text:
I've found all three problems. Two are outright bugs; the third is the genuine design choice you're pointing at.

**1. Nothing happens at the end** — [match.js:394](web/static/js/match.js:394) just flips the status line to "X wins the series 3–1", disables Pause/Stop, and reveals a `New Match` button. That button is the *last* element in the info panel, below the win-rate chart and the results list, so it's usually off-screen. Meanwhile a human game pops a proper `game-over-modal`. The two halves are inconsistent.

**2. You genuinely can't get back** — [match.js:52](web/static/js/match.js:52) decides which panel to show with `const live = !!matchId;`, and `matchId` is only ever cleared inside the `New Match` click handler. So after a match ends, clicking the **Bot vs Bot** tab always re-shows the finished board, never the picker. If you don't find that one button, the only escape is a page reload. That's the bug.

**3. The tabs model the modes as exclusive views, but a match is a server-side background thread.** Switching to *You vs Bot* mid-match doesn't stop anything — the match keeps playing and polling keeps running, with zero indication anywhere. You can start a human game while a match is still going.

Before I build the fix, the third one branches:

questions.question: A bot-vs-bot match runs server-side and keeps going whether or not you're looking at it. What should the tabs do while one is live?

options.label: Show live state on the tab (Recommended)
options.description: Keep both tabs switchable, but the Bot vs Bot tab shows a live indicator — e.g. '🤖 Bot vs Bot ● 2/4' while running, '✓ done' when finished. Clicking it always returns you to the match. Honest about the fact that it's a background job, and you can play your own game while bots grind through a series.

options.label: Lock the other tab while running
options.description: Disable the You vs Bot tab (greyed, with a tooltip) until the match finishes or is stopped. Simplest mental model — one thing at a time — but you lose the ability to play while a series runs, and it needs a clear way to stop.

options.label: Replace tabs with a Play launcher
options.description: Drop the two tabs. The Play page becomes a launcher listing 'New game vs bot', 'New bot vs bot match', and any matches currently in progress. Biggest change, but scales if you ever want several concurrent matches — the backend already supports them.

questions.question: How should the end of a match announce itself?

options.label: Result modal, like human games (Recommended)
options.description: Reuse the existing game-over modal pattern: final series score, per-bot Elo change, and buttons for 'New Match' / 'Review Games' / 'Close'. Consistent with what a human game already does, and impossible to miss.

options.label: Inline summary banner
options.description: A prominent banner at the top of the info panel instead of a modal, with the same actions. Less interruptive, stays out of the way if you're watching the final board position — but easier to overlook.

options.label: Both: banner plus a one-time toast
options.description: Inline banner that persists, plus a transient toast so you notice even if you're on the other tab. More moving parts to maintain.

Clicking it always returns you to the match. Honest about the fact that it's a background job, and you can play your own game while bots grind through a series.

options.label: Lock the other tab while running
options.description: Disable the You vs Bot tab (greyed, with a tooltip) until the match finishes or is stopped. Simplest mental model — one thing at a time — but you lose the ability to play while a series runs, and it needs a clear way to stop.

options.label: Replace tabs with a Play launcher
options.description: Drop the two tabs. The Play page becomes a launcher listing 'New game vs bot', 'New bot vs bot match', and any matches currently in progress. Biggest change, but scales if you ever want several concurrent matches — the backend already supports them.

options.label: Inline summary banner

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
run_server.py — Start the Go AI web server.

Usage:
    python run_server.py [--port PORT] [--debug]
"""

import argparse
import sys
import os

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))


def main():
    from web.app import create_app, socketio
    
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Go AI Web Server")
    parser.add_argument('--port', type=int, default=5000, help='Port to run on')
    parser.add_argument('--debug', action='store_true', help='Enable debug mode')
    args = parser.parse_args()

    app = create_app()
    print(f"\n🎯 Go AI server starting on http://localhost:{args.port}")
    print("   → Dashboard: http://localhost:{}/".format(args.port))
    print("   → Play:      http://localhost:{}/play".format(args.port))
    print("   → Training:  http://localhost:{}/training/\n".format(args.port))

    socketio.run(app, host='0.0.0.0', port=args.port, debug=args.debug,
                 allow_unsafe_werkzeug=True)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
